Titus 1.summary: Paul introduces himself as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, sent to promote the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth that accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life promised long ago by God, who never lies, and now made known through the preaching entrusted to him (Titus 1:1-3). He greets Titus as his 'true child in a common faith' (Titus 1:4). He reminds Titus that he left him in Crete to put in order what remained and to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5). Elders must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, with believing children who are not accused of wildness, and as God's stewards, overseers must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, drunk, violent or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright and committed to the trustworthy word so that they can teach sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it (Titus 1:6-9). Many people there, especially 'those of the circumcision,' are insubordinate talkers and deceivers who must be silenced because they are upsetting whole households for shameful gain (Titus 1:10-11). Paul quotes a saying of a Cretan prophet that Cretans are 'always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons,' says the testimony is true, and tells Titus to rebuke them sharply so that they may be sound in the faith and not devote themselves to Jewish myths and human commands (Titus 1:12-14). To the pure all things are pure, but the defiled and unbelieving, who profess to know God but deny him by their works, are detestable, disobedient and unfit for any good work (Titus 1:15-16).
Titus 1.whereWeAre:
Paul and Titus had been in Crete, and Paul had left Titus there to organize the churches (1:5). The letter does not say how the churches began or how long Paul stayed.

Titus was to appoint elders in every town (1:5), which implies believers were present in a number of towns. Crete was traditionally said to have had a hundred cities (Homer, Iliad 2.649), though the letter simply says 'every town.'

False teaching, linked with circumcision and Jewish myths, was spreading and upsetting households (1:10-11, 1:14).

Early Christian tradition (for example Eusebius, Church History 3.4.6) says Titus became the first bishop of the churches of Crete. This tradition comes centuries later and cannot be verified from the New Testament. The need for leaders and for guarding against deceptive teachers fits a new, scattered set of congregations where order and teaching had to be set up. The reference to the Cretans' reputation explains Paul's frankness about the obstacles.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Writes to instruct Titus, recalling his earlier directions to him. His apostolic authority stands behind Titus's work.

keyFigures.name: Titus
keyFigures.role: The one left in Crete to put things in order and appoint elders. The letter is addressed to him as Paul's delegate.

keyFigures.name: God (the Father, our Savior)
keyFigures.role: The source of the promise and of the commission. The reliability of God's word grounds the hope.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Named in the greeting and as the one served by Paul. Gives the context of the apostolic mission.

keyFigures.name: God's elect
keyFigures.role: The people for whom the apostle works. Shows the purpose of Paul's mission.

keyFigures.name: Elders and overseers (to be appointed)
keyFigures.role: Their qualifications are listed. The chapter focuses on their character and teaching.

keyFigures.name: The elder's family (wife and children)
keyFigures.role: Their conduct is part of the elder's qualifications. Reflects that leadership was tied to household life.

keyFigures.name: The false teachers
keyFigures.role: The opposition Titus must silence and rebuke. Their activity is the reason for the letter's urgency.

keyFigures.name: Whole households
keyFigures.role: Being upset by false teaching. Show the community-level damage.

keyFigures.name: The Cretans and their 'prophet'
keyFigures.role: Provide the quotation describing the culture. The quotation explains the challenges Titus faces.

keyFigures.name: Epimenides (tradition, background)
keyFigures.role: Background for the quotation. Identification is by later tradition and not by the text.

keyThemes.explanation:
Elders are to be above reproach in marriage, family, temperament, hospitality and self-control.

Those who lead God's people should be known for integrity.

Leaders must hold firm to the trustworthy word so that they can teach sound doctrine and rebuke opponents.

Faithful leadership includes both teaching and correcting.

Eternal life was promised by God, who never lies, and made known through the preaching entrusted to Paul.

The hope of the gospel rests on God's reliability.

keyThemes.theme: The danger of deceptive teaching for gain
keyThemes.explanation:
Insubordinate teachers are upsetting households and teaching for shameful gain.

Teaching should be tested by its truth and by the motives behind it.

Those who profess to know God but deny him by their works are called detestable and unfit for any good work.

Faith is shown by conduct.

Titus 2.summary: Paul tells Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine (Titus 2:1). Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified and self-controlled, sound in faith, love and steadfastness (Titus 2:2). Older women are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to wine, but teachers of what is good so that they may train the younger women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind and submissive to their own husbands, 'that the word of God may not be reviled' (Titus 2:3-5). Younger men are to be self-controlled, and Titus himself is to be a model of good works, with integrity, dignity and sound speech so that opponents are put to shame and have nothing evil to say about 'us' (Titus 2:6-8). Bondservants are to be submissive to their masters in everything, well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering but showing good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior (Titus 2:9-10). The basis for these instructions is that 'the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,' training believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives while waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,' who gave himself to redeem them from lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works (Titus 2:11-14). Titus is to declare these things, exhorting and rebuking with authority, and let no one disregard him (Titus 2:15).
Titus 2.whereWeAre:
Paul was concerned about how outsiders viewed the believers: the word of God must not be reviled, opponents were to be put to shame, and the teaching was to be made attractive (2:5, 2:8, 2:10). The letter does not describe the opposition in detail.

Roman writers often suspected new religious groups of undermining the household and public order. An example is Livy's account of the Bacchanalia affair of 186 BC (Livy 39.8-19), where an unfamiliar cult was viewed as a threat. Ancient critics later accused Christians of similar things. Whether this applied to the Cretan churches is not stated.

Slavery was widespread in the Roman Empire, and slaves were part of the early churches (compare 1 Corinthians 7:21-22; Philemon).

False teaching was active in the Cretan churches (1:10-16), so the church needed a positive pattern of life. In a world where the household was the foundation of society and where new groups were suspected, the instructions about family life and social conduct addressed how the churches could be seen as respectable and attractive, while remaining faithful.

keyFigures.name: Titus
keyFigures.role: Told to teach each group and to be a model of good works. His own conduct is part of the message.

keyFigures.name: Older men
keyFigures.role: To be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled and sound in faith, love and steadfastness. Provide examples of maturity.

keyFigures.name: Older women
keyFigures.role: To model reverent behavior and train younger women. Teaching is given a role within the community.

keyFigures.name: Younger women
keyFigures.role: To be trained in love for family, self-control, purity and kindness. Their conduct is tied to the reputation of the gospel.

keyFigures.name: Younger men
keyFigures.role: To be self-controlled. Included in the pattern of age groups.

keyFigures.name: Bondservants and their masters
keyFigures.role: Slaves are told to be submissive, honest and well-pleasing. Their conduct can adorn the doctrine.

keyFigures.name: Opponents / outsiders
keyFigures.role: Their criticism is to be answered by good conduct. Shows the missionary concern behind the instructions.

keyFigures.name: God our Savior / the grace of God
keyFigures.role: The source of salvation and of the training in godliness. The gospel is the basis of all the instructions.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: The object of hope and the one who redeemed. Provides the center of the chapter's theology.

keyFigures.name: A people for his own possession
keyFigures.role: Redeemed to be zealous for good works. Describes the church's identity.

keyThemes.explanation:
Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine, and to teach by example.

Teaching and living are meant to go together.

keyThemes.theme: Every age and station has a part
keyThemes.explanation:
Instructions are given to older men and women, younger women and men, and bondservants.

Maturity includes passing on wisdom across generations.

Good conduct prevents the word of God being reviled, puts opponents to shame, and adorns the doctrine of God.

Daily life can make the gospel attractive or discredit it.

The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation and training believers to renounce ungodliness.

God's grace not only forgives but also shapes a changed life.

keyThemes.theme: Blessed hope and a redeemed people
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers wait for the appearing of Jesus Christ, who redeemed and purified a people zealous for good works.

Hope in Christ's return and gratitude for redemption motivate good works.

Titus 3.summary: Paul tells Titus to remind the believers to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, and to be gentle and show perfect courtesy to all (Titus 3:1-2). He reminds them that they themselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray and enslaved to passions, living in malice and envy (Titus 3:3). But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved them, not because of works done in righteousness but according to his mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, they might become heirs in hope of eternal life (Titus 3:4-7). This is a trustworthy saying, and Titus is to insist on it so that believers devote themselves to good works, which are excellent and profitable, while avoiding foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions and quarrels about the law (Titus 3:8-9). A person who stirs up division is to be warned once and then twice, and then avoided (Titus 3:10-11). Paul asks Titus to come to him at Nicopolis, where he plans to spend the winter, when he sends Artemas or Tychicus, and to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way so that they lack nothing (Titus 3:12-13). He ends by urging 'our people' to learn to devote themselves to good works to meet urgent needs, sending greetings and the benediction 'Grace be with you all' (Titus 3:14-15).
Titus 3.whereWeAre:
Paul planned to spend the winter at Nicopolis and asked Titus to join him there (3:12). Sea travel in the Mediterranean was largely suspended in the winter months in antiquity, which may explain why Paul planned to stay in one place; the late fourth-century Roman writer Vegetius places the closed sailing season roughly from November to March (De re militari 4.39). Acts 27:9-12 also shows winter sailing was considered dangerous.

Nicopolis in Epirus was founded by Octavian (later Augustus) after his victory at Actium in 31 BC and became a leading city of western Greece (Strabo 7.7.6). Whether that is the Nicopolis of the letter is uncertain.

Christian teachers traveled and relied on local support, as seen in 3:13 and in 3 John 1:5-8.

Titus was told to avoid controversies about genealogies and quarrels about the law (3:9) and to deal with divisive people (3:10-11). The call for gentleness and good citizenship addresses a church that needed to be respected by outsiders. The travel arrangements and requests for support show how the early church functioned through relationships and mutual aid.

keyFigures.name: Titus
keyFigures.role: Told to remind the believers, insist on good works, avoid disputes, and come to Nicopolis. The one responsible for carrying out the instructions.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Gives instructions and travel plans. His plans show the practical network of early Christian ministry.

keyFigures.name: Rulers and authorities
keyFigures.role: Believers are to be submissive and obedient to them. Shows the church's expected posture toward government.

keyFigures.name: All people
keyFigures.role: The recipients of gentleness and courtesy. Extends the call to goodness beyond the church.

keyFigures.name: 'We' (the believers in their former state)
keyFigures.role: Described as foolish, disobedient and enslaved to passions. Used as the reason for humility and gentleness.

keyFigures.name: God our Savior
keyFigures.role: The source of salvation. The turning point of the chapter's argument.

keyFigures.name: The Holy Spirit
keyFigures.role: Brings renewal. An essential part of salvation in the passage.

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ our Savior
keyFigures.role: The mediator of salvation. Called 'Savior' as in 1:4 and 2:13.

keyFigures.name: The divisive person
keyFigures.role: To be warned twice and then avoided. Shows how the community should protect its unity.

keyFigures.name: Artemas
keyFigures.role: One of the two Paul says he will send to Titus. Shows that Paul worked with a team.

keyFigures.name: Tychicus
keyFigures.role: The other person Paul may send. Shows Paul's use of trusted envoys.

keyFigures.name: Zenas the lawyer
keyFigures.role: To be sent on his way with all he needs. Illustrates the support of traveling ministers.

keyFigures.name: Apollos
keyFigures.role: To be sent on his way with all he needs. Links the letter to a wider circle of ministers.

keyFigures.name: 'Our people'
keyFigures.role: To learn to devote themselves to good works to meet urgent needs. The chapter ends with its practical application.

keyFigures.name: Those with Paul and those who love them in the faith
keyFigures.role: Exchange greetings. Shows the network of Christian communities.

keyThemes.theme: Good citizenship and gentleness toward all
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to be submissive to authorities, speak evil of no one, avoid quarreling, and show courtesy to all.

Faith is expected to be visible in gentle and law-abiding conduct.

Believers were once foolish, disobedient and enslaved to passions.

Remembering one's own past encourages patience with others.

God saved according to his mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, so that they are justified by grace and become heirs.

Salvation is God's gift, not a reward for good deeds.

keyThemes.theme: Good works as the fitting response
keyThemes.explanation:
Believers are to devote themselves to good works, which are excellent and profitable, including helping cases of urgent need.

Grace is meant to result in practical goodness.

Believers should avoid foolish controversies and warn a divisive person twice before avoiding him.

Not every argument deserves attention, and persistent divisiveness has consequences.
